CON CLU SION ....

To THE HONORABLE JOHN G. ROBERTS, JR., CHIEF JUSTICE OF THE UNITED
STATES AND CIRCUIT JUSTICE FOR THE DISTRICT OF COLUMBIA CIRCUIT:
Plaintiffs opposition confirms that a stay of the mandate is warranted to allow this
Court to consider Ms. Herridge's petition for certiorari before an order forcing her to turn
over the identity of (presumptively) a U.S. government official to a former colonel in the
Chinese PLA takes effect. Both courts below gave themselves the opportunity to decide
the critical First Amendment issues here before that unprecedented disclosure order took
effect. This Court should give itself the same opportunity.
First, Plaintiff fails to rebut Ms. Herridge's straightforward showing that this Court
is reasonably likely to grant certiorari because this case implicates two distinct circuit
splits: one on the standards for applying the First Amendment reporter's privilege and
another on whether to recognize a non-constitutional reporters' privilege under Federal
Rule of Evidence 501. This Court's guidance is needed on both issues. Plaintiffs suggestion
that the district court supposedly already held that Ms. Herridge would fall short even
under her preferred First Amendment test (Opp. 13—19) misrepresents the record.
Plaintiff floated that argument below in opposition to Ms. Herridge's motion for a stay
pending interlocutory appeal, and the district court itself rejected the argument. The
district court flatly stated that it "remains possible that any refinement of the applicable
test by the Circuit on appeal would alter the result." Chen v. FBI, No. 18-cv-3074, 2023 WL
6461011, at *I (D.D.C. Sept. 6, 2023). That is equally true of any refinements from this
Court.
Second, there is a fair prospect that this Court would reverse the D.C. Circuit on at
1

least one of the questions presented. Plaintiff cannot avoid the fact that the D.C. Circuit's
approach to the First Amendment privilege boils down to a mere exhaustion requirement
under which a plaintiffs need always trumps the privilege. That is no privilege at all. There
is little reason to think this Court would take such a miserly view of the First Amendment,
contrary to the majority of circuits that have addressed the issue, especially when this case
so well illustrates the perverse consequences of the rule. When a constitutional privilege
forces a reporter to turn over the identity of a U.S. government official to a former PLA
colonel so that she can pursue a civil claim against the U.S. government under the Privacy
Act, something is seriously awry. And even if this Court affirmed a decision reducing the
constitutional privilege to an exhaustion requirement, the Court would still likely adopt a
broader non-constitutional privilege under Rule 501, drawing on the near-uniform
consensus among the states as Rule 501 expressly authorizes.
Third, there can be no dispute that Ms. Herridge faces irreparable harm absent a
stay. Without a stay, she will either be forced to disclose her source(s), which Plaintiff does
not dispute is a quintessential irreparable harm, or be held in contempt backed by fines
currently set at $800 a day. And notwithstanding Plaintiffs novel theory, this Court should
not simply assume that Ms. Herridge will incur those fines and essentially preserve this
Court's ability to adjudicate her certiorari petition on pain of contempt. A stay exists
precisely to avoid situations where the only possibility for avoiding irreparable harm and
preserving this Court's ability to consider a petition is to go into contempt. Regardless,
being forced to pay daily fines for exercising one's First Amendment rights—in effect, a
pay-as-you-go access fee for the Constitution—is itself an obvious and unambiguous
2

infringement on the First Amendment, which this Court's cases have for decades
recognized as an irreparable injury. All the more so when the fees could, in total, amount
to "hundreds of thousands of dollars of fines." App. 50a. Not a single case holds otherwise.
Finally, Plaintiff cannot and does not identify any material harm that would befall
her as a result of a stay. A stay here would simply preserve the status quo that allowed the
district court and court of appeals to adjudicate these consequential issues without
contempt sanctions piling up or an appeal-mooting disclosure. Indeed, the court of appeals
took over two and a half years to resolve this appeal with a stay in place. Extending the
stay for a much shorter period to allow this Court to consider these critical issues makes
eminent sense and clearly serves the public interest.
The bottom line in this case is that Ms. Herridge lived up to the highest standards
of her profession, fulfilled the key role of the press in our democracy, and performed a
public service by exposing what DOD later determined was a genuine national security
threat. But under the D.C. Circuit's cramped view of the First Amendment, her reward is
the brutal dilemma of choosing between disclosing her confidential source(s)—and thereby
breaching the trust essential to her career as an investigative journalist—or suffering
crippling fines. Absent a stay, Ms. Herridge will be forced to that choice before this Court
even has an opportunity to decide whether it should review the D.C. Circuit's decision.
None of that has anything to recommend it. The Court should stay the mandate from the
D.C. Circuit so that it may consider the petition for a writ of certiorari in the ordinary
course.
3

ARGUMENT
Contrary to Plaintiffs assertions, Ms. Herridge does not face an "especially heavy
burden" (Opp. 2) in seeking this stay. The applicable standard is well-settled: The Court
considers whether there is "(I) a reasonable probability that four Justices will consider the
issue sufficiently meritorious to grant certiorari; (2) a fair prospect that a majority of the
Court will vote to reverse the judgment below; and (3) a likelihood that irreparable harm
will result from the denial of a stay," without placing any especially heavy burdens on the
stay applicant. Hollingsworth v. Perry, 558 U.S. 183, 190 (2010) (per curiam). As Plaintiffs
own cited cases illustrate, her elevated standard applies only where an applicant seeks a
stay of a district court order from this Court after being rebuffed by the lower courts. See,
e.g., Edwards v. Hope Medical Group for Women, 512 U.S. 1301, 1302 (1994) (Scalia, J., in
chambers). I This case involves almost the opposite situation, where the lower courts have
granted a stay pending appeal and kept that stay in place to facilitate appellate review. In
that circumstance, no heightened standard applies, and the lower courts' actions strongly
suggest that at least one of the factors this Court considers—irreparable harm—is
satisfied. Regardless, this is such a quintessential situation for a stay that all the factors
favor a stay under either standard.
1.
There Is a Reasonable Probability this Court Will Grant Certiorari.
As Ms. Herridge explained in her application to this Court, there is a reasonable
1 Beame v. Friends of the Earth, 434 U.S. 1310, 1312 (1977) (Marshall, J., in chambers), is similarly off
point. There, the mandate from the court of appeals had issued months earlier, the district court had already
entered an order on remand implementing that decision, and it was effectively the district court's new order
that the applicant was seeking to stop. ld; see also Friends oftheEarthv. Carey, 76 F.R.D. 33, 37 (S.D.N.Y.
1977) (showing that request for a stay started in district court).
4

probability that this Court will grant her petition for a ywit of certiorari because this case
squarely implicates two separate and longstanding circuit splits on important issues of
national significance. App.15a—23a. Plaintiffs efforts to undermine the likelihood of
plenary review all fail.
A. The District Court Did Not Enter an Alternative Holding Applying a
Broader Balancing Test Under the First Amendment Privilege.
Plaintiffs primary argument why the Court is unlikely to grant review rests on a
blatant misstatement of the record. Contrary to Plaintiffs assertions (Opp. 13—19), the
district court did not enter an alternative holding applying the comprehensive balancing
analysis that Ms. Herridge advocated. Instead, the district court squarely anchored its
analysis on only "two guideposts: centrality and exhaustion," App. 33a, and held that "those
two factors are dispositive," id 40a. To be sure, in denying Ms. Herridge's motion to quash,
the district court went on to suggest, "for the sake of completeness," that considering other
factors in the balance "likely would not change the outcome." ld. 22a (emphasis added).
But the district court itself made clear that "this prediction 'wUs far from conclusive."
Chen, 2023 WL 6461011, at *1 (emphasis added). Indeed, the district court emphasized that
"[i]t thus remains possible that any refinement of the applicable test by the Circuit on
appeal would alter the result." ld. That is consistent with this Court's repeated recognition
that predictive judgments are not the same thing as an actual analysis applying the
governing test as refined by this Court. Cf Mullin v. Doe, 2026 WL 1825840, at *11 (U.S.
June 25, 2026) (plurality op.) (describing comparable "likelihood of success" analysis as
"mak[ing] only a predictive—not a final—decision about the outcome of the case"). Simply
5

put, the district court itself expressly disavowed the alternative holding that Plaintiff is now
trying to attribute to it.
In the Contempt Order, the district court similarly included a terse discussion about
the likely outcome of weighing other factors, but in staying that order it again repeated the
view that the "Circuit may ... refine the applicable First Amendment test in Herridge's
favor," App. 50a—which could change the outcome of the case. The stay would have been
pointless if Plaintiff were right and the district court believed it had already applied Ms.
Herridge's test, such that any "refinement" of the test on appeal would be meaningless.
Thus, the district court itself acknowledged (again) that it had not made an alternative
holding foreclosing Ms. Herridge's arguments about the proper test for the reporter's
privilege. If anyone is "hid[ing] the ball" (Opp. 13) about what the district court said, it is
Plaintiff.
In addition, to the extent the district court set out a cursory discussion of what a
broader balancing "likely" would look like, it clearly was not applying the full balancing
analysis that Ms. Herridge called for. For example, the passage Plaintiff cites as supposed
evidence that the district court considered factors like the limited value of Plaintiffs Privacy
Act claim shows the opposite. The district court rejected such an analysis because it would
"exceed[]" the "cursory inspection" of the merits that it believed was authorized under D.C.
Circuit precedent. App. 41a.
Further, part of the test Ms. Herridge sought would require examining elements of
Plaintiffs case on summary judgment. The district court squarely rejected that analysis.
See App. 22a; id. 34a (insisting it was "premature to preview summary judgment").
6

Moreover, the whole point of testing Plaintiffs case on partial summary judgment (or
motions in limine to exclude evidence of certain categories of damages) would be to narrow
the case to establish that Plaintiff was likely to recover no damages or at most nominal
damages. And that matters, because under a genuine balancing approach, it would make
no sense to force the disclosure of a reporter's confidential sources in support of claim worth
only a nominal amount. The district court, however, even in its hypothetical consideration
of other factors, proceeded on the view that, if any part of Plaintiffs claim could survive,
the First Amendment reporter's privilege would always lose. See id. 23a; id. 41a. That does
not reflect even a hypothetical application of a balancing test. Instead, that outcome reflects
an absolute rule that, if a plaintiff needs access to a confidential source even for a nominal
claim, the plaintiff always gets access. Nothing could be further from the rule Ms. Herridge
sought to have the courts apply.
The D.C. Circuit, moreover, did not engage in any further balancing analysis—even
in musings in dicta—and it also decided the case on the express assumption that even a
claim for "as little as $1,000 in statutory damages," id. 61a, would overcome the First
Amendment privilege. That decision leads directly to the anomalous situation here where
Ms. Herridge faces daily contempt sanctions that potentially approximate the entire value
of the plaintiffs claim. That is absurd. A decision from this Court adopting a genuine
balancing analysis for the privilege would plainly require redoing that analysis and almost
certainly change the outcome in the case.
7

B. The Court Would Likely Grant Review to Resolve the Circuit Conflict on
the First Amendment Privilege.
Once Plaintiffs illusory "alternative holding" theory is debunked, it is plain that the
circuit conflict concerning the First Amendment privilege warrants review by this Court.
Plaintiffs claim that the circuit split Ms. Herridge identifies is "fanciful" (Opp. 3) simply
ignores the content of the cases making up the split. As Ms. Herridge has explained, the
D.C. Circuit's test for applying the First Amendment reporter's privilege—under which
the privilege is always overcome if (1) the information sought from a reporter is central to
the case ("centrality"), and (2) the movant has exhausted other sources of information
("exhaustion"), (App. 62a—63a)—conflicts with the tests applied by multiple other circuits
and state supreme courts. Plaintiff's efforts to explain away the conflicts follow a pattern.
She isolates a snippet of language from an opinion addressing factors similar to centrality
and exhaustion and then ignores directives explaining that those factors do not stand alone
and that courts must also engage in a broader balancing of interests. That gets plaintiff
nowhere, as no one is suggesting that centrality and exhaustion are irrelevant, but the
circuits are plainly split on whether those two factors are the only factors or just two factors
to consider in a broader balancing.
For example, Plaintiff notes that in Bruno & Stillman, Inc. v. Globe Newspaper Co.,
633 F.2d 583 (1st Cir. 1980), the First Circuit identified "centrality, exhaustion, and non-
frivolousness" as factors to consider. Opp. 19—20. Of course they are. But Bruno
immediately explained that those factors were not an exclusive list of the "inquiries [that]
should be made by the court," and that, instead, "[t]he task is one that demands sensitivity,
8

invites flexibility, and defies formula." Bruno, 633 F.2d at 598. Plaintiff has no response to
the First Circuit's insistence that the Bruno test "contemplates consideration of a myriad
of factors, often uniquely drawn out of the factual circumstances of the particular case."
Cusumano Q). Microsoft Corp., 162 F.3d 708, 716 (1st Cir. 1998). In particular, as Ms.
Herridge pointed out, the First Circuit specifically instructs that courts should "assess[]"
"the importance to the [journalist's] continued newsgathering effectiveness of preserving
the source's confidentiality," Bruno, 633 F.2d at 597—98, a factor the D.C. Circuit squarely
refused to consider. Plaintiff ignores this language. Plaintiff also has no good answer for
the First Circuit's instruction that courts must consider whether disclosure of a particular
source might cause "harm ... disproportionate to a plaintiffs litigation needs." ld. at 595.
Under Plaintiffs reading, Bruno prohibited the exact proportionality analysis it claimed to
be mandating.
Plaintiff also distorts Bruno by claiming that, when the First Circuit repeatedly
instructed that a plaintiff must show "jury issues" on the essential elements of its case, it
was not referring to summary judgment and, instead, was simply repeating the
requirement that the case must not be frivolous. Opp. 20—21. That is nonsense. The First
Circuit made clear it was identifying distinct requirements as it set out a virtual checklist,
explaining that, even where (1) "the case does not appear frivolous," (2) there "appears to
be a jury issue" on essential elements, and (3) "the desired information appears more than
remotely relevant," the court still must pursue a further inquiry to "assess the extent to
which there is a need for confidentiality." Bruno, 633 F.2d at 597. In fact, the First Circuit
made it express that courts should consider summary judgment before ordering disclosure,
9

instructing that courts "defer disclosure ... until more discovery has taken place with the
possibility that summary judgment would be appropriate." ld. at 598 (emphasis added).
Postponing disclosure until elements of Plaintiffs case could be tested on summary
judgment is exactly what Ms. Herridge sought in this case and the D.C. Circuit refused to
contemplate.
Plaintiff similarly distorts the Fourth Circuit's test. She focuses solely on the fact
that the Fourth Circuit has identified (1) relevance, (2) exhaustion, and (3) whether the
plaintiff has a "compelling interest" in the information as factors to be considered. Opp.
21-22 (citing Ashcraft v. Conoco, Inc., 218 F.3d 282, 287 (4th Cir. 2000)). But she ignores
the Fourth Circuit's holding that, even when those factors are satisfied, "the compelling
nature of the interest [in disclosure] would have to be balanced against the reporter's
interest in protecting the confidentiality of his sources" before disclosure is ordered.
Ashcraft, 218 F.3d at 287—88 & n.12. That is precisely the balancing of interests that the
panel in this case refused to perform.
Plaintiffs characterizations of the law in the Ninth and Tenth Circuits are similarly
misplaced. Opp. 22. She again points to language discussing factors such as centrality and
exhaustion—again, factors all agree are relevant—but ignores the instruction that those
two factors are not dispositive and courts must engage in more comprehensive balancing.
Shoen v. Shoen, 5 F.3d 1289 (9th Cir. 1993), explained that the "First Amendment privilege
and the opposing need for disclosure [must] be judicially weighed in light of the surrounding
facts, and a balance struck to determine where lies the paramount interest." ld. at 1292—
93. It then went on to consider additional factors that "diminish[] the journalist's, and the
10

public's, interest in nondisclosure." ld. at 1295. As for the Tenth Circuit, Grandbouche v.
Clancy, 825 F.2d 1463 (10th Cir. 1987) explained that the listed factors are "[a]mong the
factors that the trial court must consider" and that the court still must decide "whether the
privilege must be overborne by the need for the requested information" after considering
the enumerated factors. ld. at 1466-67.
Finally, Plaintiff's interpretation of McKevitt v. Pallasch, 339 F.3d 530 (7th Cir.
2003) (Posner, J.)—which she claims did not deepen the split in authority by rejecting the
privilege—defies the Seventh Circuit's (and McKevitt's author's) understanding of the case.
U.S. Dep't of v. Nat'l Collegiate Athletic Ass'n, 481 F.3d 936, 938 (7th Cir. 2007)
(Posner, J.) (citing McKevitt for the proposition that "[t]here isn't even a reporter's
privilege in federal cases"); see also, e.g., (Jruz v. Guevara, 801 F. Supp. 3d 767, 774 (N.D.
III. 2024) ("[N]o federal reporter's privilege exists in the Seventh Circuit."); Beverly v.
Watson, No. 14-cv-4970, 408 U.L 3633316, at *5 (N.D. 111. July 7, 2016) (same); Thayer v.
Chiczewski, 257 F.R.D. 466, 468 (N.D. 111. 2009) (same). There is a reason all those
authorities disagree with Plaintiff: McKevitt is crystal clear in rejecting the existence of a
First Amendment privilege. 339 F Bd at 532—33 (finding it "surprising" that some courts
recognize a privilege after Branzburg and instructing that "rather than speaking of
privilege, courts should simply make sure that a subpoena . directed to the media, like any
other subpoena ... is reasonable").
Plaintiff also mischaracterizes state decisions. First, Plaintiff dismisses lure Grand
Jury Proc. (Ridenhour), 520 So. 2d 372 (La. 1988), merely because it cites Zerilli as an
example of a case recognizing the privilege, despite the fact that the case plainly calls for a
11

comprehensive balancing of interests. ld. at 376. Next, Plaintiff claims that In re Letellier,
578 A.2d 722, 726 (Me. 1990), is inapposite because it endorsed balancing in a criminal case.
That argument cuts against Plaintiff—courts generally apply a less protective version of
the privilege in criminal cases. The case Plaintiff cites to support her argument makes this
point clear, as the court, faced with a civil action, went beyond Letellier's balancing test and
added Bruno's requirement that Plaintiff show a jury issue on the essential elements of its
case. Levesque v. Doocy, 247 F.R.D. 55, 57—58 (D. Me. 2007) (granting motion to quash for
failure to show jury issues). Other state courts have adopted a balancing test as well. See,
e.g., State 'b'. Davis, 720 So. 2d 220, 224 (Fla. 1998) (requiring courts to weigh the parties'
interests as part of its "compelling need" factor); Mitchell v. Superior Ct., 690 P.2d 625, 634
(Cal. 1984) (listing "the importance of protecting confidentiality in the case at hand" as a
factor to be weighed).
Finally, there is no merit to Plaintiffs argument that Ms. Herridge has made an
"opportunistic shift" (Opp. 24) by asserting a conflict among the circuits only after the D.C.
Circuit panel issued its decision. That claim is doubly misguided: First, what mattered in
the D.C. Circuit was D.C. Circuit precedent, see LaShawn A. 'v. Barry, 87 F.3d 1389, 1395
(D.C. Cir. 1996), which Ms. Herridge addressed at length below. Aplt. Br. at 22—29, Chen
v. FBI, No. 24-5050 (D.C. Cir. June 26, 2024). And second, the circuit conflict was created
by the D.C. Circuit's novel and cramped understanding of First Amendment protections in
this case; there was no occasion to inform the court of a circuit split that did not yet exist.
Once the panel created the split, Ms. Herridge promptly raised it to the court in her next
filing—her petition for rehearing en banc—as even Plaintiff acknowledges.
12

c.
There Is a Reasonable Probability the Court Will Grant Certiorari to
Resolve the Conflict on the Common Law Reporter's Privilege under
Rule 501.
Plaintiffs assertions that the Court would not grant certiorari to address the
existence of a non-constitutional reporter's privilege under Rule 501 also miss the mark.
First, contrary to Plaintiffs claims, nothing in Branzbwrg v. Hayes, 408 U.S. 665
(1972), which rejected an absolute First Amendment reporter's privilege in the cHminal
context, bars recognition of a common law reporter's privilege (whether absolute or
qualified) in civil cases. Indeed, much has changed since this Court decided Branztyurg in
1972. In 1975, Congress enacted Rule 501 of the Federal Rules of Evidence, which
affirmatively invites federal courts to define new privileges by interpreting "[t]he common
law ... in the light of reason and experience." As this Court has explained, Rule 501 reflects
Congress' "affirmative intention not to freeze the law of privilege," but to "leave the door
open to change," Trammel 'v. United States, 445 U.S. 40, 47 (1980), and the evolutionary
development of testimonial privileges." Jaffee v. Redmond, 518 U.S. I, 9 (1996). And while
only 17 states recognized a reporteFs privilege when the Court decided Branzburg, see 408
U .S. at 689 n.27, virtually every state recognizes the privilege today. That consensus
"indicates that 'reason and experience' support recognition of the privilege." ld. at 13.2
Second, Plaintiffs attempt to claim that there is no split in authority between the
Third Circuit—which recognizes a common law privilege—and the D.C. Circuit—which
refuses to do so—fails. Plaintiff contends that the Third Circuit's reporter's privilege test,
2 The criminal cases Plaintiff cites similarly inapposite. United States v. Sterling, 724 F.3d 482 (4th Cir. 2013);
In re Grand Jury Procs., 5 F.3d 397 (9th Cir. 1993). Both found themselves bound by Branzburg and invoked
the importance of enforcing the criminal laws as part of their analyses.
13

regardless of its basis, is identical to the D.C. Circuit's test. But that claim is again an
exercise in selective quotation. In a now-familiar move, Plaintiff points to language in Riley
v. City of Chester, 612 F.2d 708 (3d Cir. 1979), instructing courts to consider factors similar
to centrality and exhaustion, which everyone agrees are relevant considerations, but
ignores the court's clear instruction that courts must "balance
... the policies which give
rise to the privilege and their applicability to the facts at hand against the need for the
evidence sought to be obtained," id. at 716—which is again something the D.C. Circuit
expressly refused to do. Plaintiffs fallback argument—that the Riley test must be identical
to the D.C. Circuit test because the D.C. Circuit has previously cited Riley—fails for the
reasons given above.
Plaintiffs argument that there is too much "vari[ation]" in state privileges to support
creating a federal analog also fails. Opp. 34. First, there is no variation on the most critical
question: whether a reporter's privilege exists in the first place. Second, variation on the
precise contours of that privilege is not fatal. In Jaffee, this Court recognized a common-
law psychotherapist's privilege despite variation in the contours of the state-level analogs.
See 518 U.S. at 12 (noting that 50 states applied "some form" of relevant privilege); see also
id. at 16 (discussing variations). Last, any variation is of little consequence here. Twenty-
three jurisdictions recognize an absolute privilege in non-defamation civil cases. Appl. 33.
Two more recognize a privilege that, although not always absolute, would be absolute in
this case because they contain only exceptions not relevant here.a Eighteen more require
3 Ark. code Ann. \16-85-510; R.I. Gen. Laws "9-19.1 to -3.
14

a comprehensive balancing of interests. 4 As does the Third Circuit's test. Riley, 612 F.2d
at 716. In other words, the states (and District of Columbia) are virtually uniform in the
only metric that matters—almost all provide a privilege that is more protective than the
rule adopted below. Were the Court to endorse even the least protective of these options
and require an actual balancing of interests, the outcome of this case would likely change.
That reality similarly disposes of Plaintiff's argument that the common law privilege would
simply mirror the D.C. Circuit's test—that claim has not been borne out in any of the
jurisdictions to have adopted a reporter's privilege, whether under statute or common law.
Finally, the fact that the Court declined to grant certiorari in Risen v. United States,
572 U.S. 1149 (2014), and Thomas v. Lee, 547 U.S. 1187 (2006), changes nothing. Risen was
a criminal case, and recognition of a reporter's privilege in the criminal context remains
rare. As for Thomas, twenty years have passed since the Court declined review in that
case. Over those twenty years, states have continued to enact or expand reporter's privilege
statutes, and their experience with the successful expansion of the privilege is a key factor
in determining whether to recognize a common law privilege. Jaffee, 518 U.S. at 12. This
Court's instruction that courts should "continue the evolutionary development of
testimonial privileges," id. at 9, would be meaningless if a twenty-year-old, unexplained
Alaska stat. "09.25.goo, .310(b); Colo. Rev. stat. \13-90-119; Conn. Gen. stat. 52-146t; State v. Davis, 720
so. 2d 220, 224 (Fla. 1998); Haw. Rev. stat. 5621-31; 735 111. comp. Stat. 5/8-907; Lamberto v. Bown, 326
N.W.2d 305, 309 (Iowa 1982); Kan. stat. Ann. 560-482; La. stat. Ann. Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 16, $1; In
John Doe Grand Jury Investigation, 574 N.E.2d 373, 375 (Mass. 1991); State Classic 111 Inc. v. Ely,
954 S.W.2d 650, 655 (Mo. ct. App. 1997); Mortg. Specialists, Inc. v. Implode-Explode Heavy Indus., Inc., 160
N.H. 227, 235-36 (2010); N.M. R. Evid. Rule 11-514; Grand Forks Herald v. Dist. Ct. in &for Grand Forks
cnty., 322 N.W.2d 850, 857 (N.D. 1982); Tenn. code Ann. *24-1-208; Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code \22.024;
Clemente v. Clemente, 56 Va. Cir. 530, at *1 (2001).
15

denial of certiorari foreclosed recognition of a privilege that nearly all the states have
adopted. Cf Stebbing v. Maryland, 469 U.S. 900, 907 (1984) (Marshall, J., dissenting) ("[l]t
is axiomatic that denials of writs of certiorari have no precedential value.").
Finally, it bears emphasis that if the Court grants review of the First Amendment
question, it would be well served to grant review on the Rule 501 question so that it would
have available both constitutional and non-constitutional grounds for decision. What makes
no sense is the holding below that there is zero protection—neither constitutional nor
common-law—for a national-security reporter forced to turn over the identity of
(presumptively) a U.S. government official at the behest of a former PLA colonel pursuing
a civil claim likely to produce at most a de minimis recovery.
II. There Is at Least a Fair Prospect that the Court Would Reverse.
A. There Is a Fair Prospect the Court Would Reject the D.C. Circuit's
Mechanical Test for the First Amendment Reporter's Privilege.
Plaintiff also fails to provide any sound basis for concluding that there is not a "fair
prospect that a majority of the Court will vote to reverse the judgment below."
Hollingsworth, 558 U.S. at 190. To the contrary, there is every reason think that a majority
of the Court would agree that the D.C. Circuit's rule reducing the reporter's privilege to a
mere exhaustion requirement provides insufficient protection for reporters and their
confidential sources. Indeed, this case perfectly illustrates the problems with that rule.
To start, Plaintiff wrongly suggests (Opp. 25) that Branzburg v. Hayes, somehow
forecloses even the possibility that reporters could be entitled to protection for their
confidential sources under the First Amendment. Every circuit to address the question
16

(except the Seventh Circuit)5 has reached the opposite conclusion. The courts of appeals
routinely cite Branzburg as support for adopting a balancing test to apply the reporter's
privilege. see, e.g., Bruno, 633 F.2d at 594; Ashcraft, 218 F.3d at 287; cf Riley, 612 F.2d at
715 (basing "federal common law privilege" on Branzbwrg). Justice Powell's concurrence
explained that the Court's decision in Branzburg "does not hold that [reporters] are without
constitutional rights with respect to ... safeguarding their sources," and he went on to
explain that such constitutional protections should be determined by applying a balancing
test. Branzburg, 408 U.S. at 709—10 (Powell, J., concurring). There is no reason to think
that a majority on this Court would reject the approach that circuits like the First Circuit
have taken to applying such a test.
Next, Plaintiff tries to pretend that the test applied by the D.C. Circuit already does
"balance[] a litigant's need for information against any potential harm that might befall
reporters." Opp. 26. But that is obviously incorrect. The D.C. Circuit's approach is an
absolute, mechanical rule under which, if a plaintiff needs a source to make his case and
cannot uncover the source by other means, the plaintiff always gets access to the source
from the reporter. The rule applies to civil and criminal cases alike, and there is no
balancing of interests involved—in fact, there is no consideration of the reporter's interests
at all. The mere fact that a plaintiff may be sent back to exhaust some other alternative
avenues of discovery first (as in Zerilli, see Opp. 26) does not alter the ultimate rule—the
plaintiff always gets the source eventually because the plaintiffs need is always treated as

trumping any First Amendment privilege.
Plaintiff also misses the point in trying to debate whether Ms. Herridge has
adequately shown in her stay application that the Privacy Act claim will likely be whittled
down to no damages or almost no damages. Opp. 27—28. The relevant point is that the
courts below refused even to consider whether Plaintiffs claims might be cut down because
they held that it was irrelevant. The D.C. Circuit decided the case on the express
assumption that Plaintiffs claim might end up being nothing more than a claim for "as little
as $1,000 in statutory damages." App. 61a. But the D.C. Circuit still thought such a trivial
claim warranted overriding the First Amendment privilege. ld. 61a—62a. There is at least
a "fair prospect" that five members of this Court would disagree with that assessment. See
Opp. 28. And that is especially true in a case like this where the evidence shows that forcing
disclosure would hobble the career of the reporter involved.
Plaintiff is similarly off base in trying to brush away the national security context of
the case, as if it is somehow "repugnant" (Opp. 29) to bring up the facts. DOD found as a
matter of fact that Plaintiff

DOI) determined that
her university were a national security threat and terminated their funding. Plaintiff then
decided not to challenge those factual findings in court. Those factual findings may well
give the government a defense in the Privacy Act case, see App. 28a—29a, and Ms.
Herridge's simple point is that defenses like that should be tested before she is required to

turn over her confidential source(s). Contrary to Plaintiffs overheated rhetoric, there
would be nothing "repugnant" about a court taking into account that Plaintiffs Privacy Act

Finally, Plaintiffs vague assertion that a genuine balancing test would somehow be
"inherently unworkable" (Opp. 26) is belied by the experience of the multiple circuits that
rely on such a test. The First Circuit, for example, explains that its balancing test "demands
sensitivity, invites flexibility, and defies formula," Bruno, 633 F.2d at 598, and that it
"contemplates consideration of a myriad of factors, often uniquely drawn out of the factual
circumstances of the particular case," Cusumano, 162 F.3d at 716. But that test has not
proven unworkable in the more than forty years it has been applied.
B. There Is a Fair Prospect that the Court Will Recognize a Common Law
Privilege Under 501.
When determining whether a common-law privilege would comport with "reason
and experience," this Court considers two main factors: (I) whether the proposed privilege
advances a "public good transcending the normally predominant principle of utilizing all
rational means for ascertaining truth," Jaffee, 518 U.S. at 9—10, and (2) the "policy decisions
of the States" with respect to state-level evidentiary privileges, id. at 12.
Plaintiff does not seriously dispute that the reporter's privilege advances a "public
19

good transcending the normally predominant principle of utilizing all rational means for
ascertaining truth"—nor could she, as the legislatures and courts of forty-eight states and
the District of Columbia, as well as nearly every U.S. court of appeals, hold differently. This
factor plainly weighs in favor of recognizing a common law reporter's privilege.
Rather than challenge the first factor, Plaintiff argues that the "policy decisions of
the States" prong does not favor creation of a privilege because there is too much variation
in how the states apply the privilege. As explained above, however, variation is not fatal.
See Jaffee, 518 U.S. at 12 (noting that 50 states applied "some form" of relevant privilege);
see also id. at 16 (discussing variations). The variations that exist, moreover, are of little
consequence here, as forty-three jurisdictions recognize a privilege that would be more
protective of Ms. Herridge than the D.C. Circuit's test. Supra Part I.C. Even the least
protective common law version of the privilege would likely change the outcome here.
Plaintiff's related argument—that a common law privilege is unnecessary because it
would mirror the D.C. Circuit's test—similarly fails. Given the importance of the policy
decisions of the states under Jaffee, there is no reason to suspect that this Court would
adopt a version of the privilege mirroring the D.C. Circuit's test. Almost no states have
adopted such a limited version of the privilege. Accordingly, the policy decisions of the
states also weigh in favor of recognizing a privilege.
Finally, Plaintiff briefly suggests that recognition of a common law reporter's
privilege would pose practical challenges (Opp. 34), but fails to answer even basic questions
like how or why. Presumably, if there were genuine practical difficulties in applying a
common law reporter's privilege, they would have surfaced sometime in the half-century
20

during which the Third Circuit has recognized one. Plaintiffs inability to articulate even
one is self-impeaching.
III. Ms. Herridge Will Suffer Irreparable Harm Absent a Stay.
Plaintiff wholly fails to rebut the obvious irreparable harm that Ms. Herridge will
suffer if the order below goes into effect. Plaintiff cannot and does not dispute that if Ms.
Herridge complies with the order and discloses her source(s) she will suffer irreparable
harm. There would be no way to undo the disclosure, and it would likely make this case
moot, thus depriving Ms. Herridge of judicial review. See, e.g., John Doe Agency v. John
Doe Corp., 488 U.s. 1306, 1309 (1989) (Marshall, J., in chambers). Instead, Plaintiff rests
entirely on the blithe suggestion (Opp. 35) that Ms. Herridge can defy the court order, pay
$800 a day, and continue to withhold her source(s). But courts do not deny otherwise
appropriate stays by assuming the applicant can simply go into contempt. Regardless, that
"option" does nothing to dispel the irreparable harm Ms. Herridge faces.
First, Plaintiff ignores the settled rule that "loss of First Amendment freedoms, for
even minimal periods of time, unquestionably constitutes irreparable injury." Roman
Catholic Diocese of Brooklyn v. Cuomo, 592 U.S. 14, 19 (2020) (quoting Elrod v. Burns, 427
U.S. 347, 373 (1976) (plurality)). Not even Plaintiff can dispute that disclosure of a
confidential source is a classic irreparable injury that cannot be undone and would likely
moot any appeal. But the First Amendment injury here is not limited to disclosing the
source(s). Being forced to pay $800 a day for the privilege of exercising one's First
Amendment rights itself infringes those rights, even if the fines are (in theory) ultimately
recoverable. It indisputably burdens those rights in a way that is wholly incompatible with
21

this Court's consistent recognition that First Amendment "freedoms are delicate and
vulnerable" and that even "[t]he threat of sanctions may deter their exercise almost as
potently as the actual application of sanctions." NAACPv. Button, 371 U.S. 415, 433 (1963).6
Second, Plaintiff does not point to a single case adopting the proposition that
mandatory disclosure orders do not impose irreparable injury simply because the fine for
violating the order might one day be recoverable on appeal. Instead, Plaintiffs cited cases
stand for nothing more than the generic proposition that recoverable economic loss is not
irreparable, without any analysis of the combined First Amendment and civil contempt
fines context presented here. 7
Moreover, it is backwards to evaluate irreparable harm on the assumption that an
applicant will simply go into contempt. After all, the whole point of contempt fines in this
context is to coerce compliance. Instead, the proper approach in analyzing whether a court
order may inflict irreparable harm turns on the harm that would flow from implementing

with an appealed order would so obviously inflict irreparable harm and moot the appeal that

I V. The Balance of Equities and Public Interest Favor a Stay.
Plaintiff is conspicuously silent about any material harm that she would suffer from
a stay—because there is no such harm. This case has been pending for over seven and a
half years. Plaintiff is seeking a confidential source for stories that were published more
than nine years ago. Even if the Court were ultimately to deny Ms. Herridge's petition for
certiorari, at this point, waiting three more months until this Court can give the petition
due consideration in the ordinary course will not affect Plaintiff's case in the slightest.
When it comes to balancing the equities, weighing Ms. Herridge's weighty First
Amendment interests against Plaintiffs nonexistent harms is easy: "something
outweighs nothing every time." SpeechNow.org FEC, 599 F.3d 686, 695 (D.C. Cir. 2010).
Last, Plaintiffs claim (Opp. 39—40) that a stay will harm the public interest in
enforcing the Privacy Act is meritless. The public has limited (if any) interest in Plaintiffs
private action to recover damages. Even assuming such a public interest exists, it strains
credulity to suggest that interest will be vindicated only if Ms. Herridge is immediately
subjected to fines and forced to disclose her source(s) in a case that is already more than
seven and a half years old. A short delay pending a petition for certiorari will have no impact
on any public interest in vindicating the Privacy Act in this case. Nor would a stay
undermine "the public interest in the enforcement of court orders" (Opp. 40), because it
would not prevent the ultimate enforcement of the underlying Contempt Order if that order
survives further review.
Properly understood, the public interest favors staying the mandate from the D.C.
Circuit, because it favors preserving First Amendment protections for reporters'
24

confidential sources that foster the free flow of information to the press. Indeed, the public
interest clearly tips in favor of a stay. The public interest in robust reporting in the national
security arena is obvious and depends on reporters being able to maintain the
confidentiality of their sources. See Reporters Comm. for Freedom of the Press Amicus
Br. 4—8. Here, for example, Ms. Herridge's reporting plainly promoted that public interest
by exposing to public scrutiny a scenario that DOD later determined was a genuine national
security threat. The public interest favors fostering the conditions that allow such
reporting to occur—including preserving First Amendment protections for reporters'
confidential sources.
CONCLUSION
The Court should stay issuance of the mandate from the D.C. Circuit.
